_comment: Few-shot examples encoding the K-VERSATION editorial style: sparse, intentional visuals for major events, named people/places, maps, documents, battles, emotional beats and topic transitions. Generic connective narration is deliberately NOT selected. Calibrated against 13 published episodes (King Sejong, Son Heung-min, APEC 2025, Korean Convenience Store, Baduk, Han River, Korean Confucianism, Kpop Demon Hunters, Culinary Class Wars, Koreans in the NFL, Stacey Milbern, ...).
style_notes: The screen is black by default; in published episodes visuals are on screen only 20-50% of the runtime.
A visual appears only when it adds information the words cannot: a face, a place, a building, an object, a document, a map, a logo, a table.
Visuals cluster at the introduction of a concrete subject (1-3 related images back-to-back, ~5 s each), then black while the narrator elaborates.

Maps at geographic transitions, portraits/press photos at first mention of a key person, documents when a text/treaty/manuscript is quoted, logos at first mention of an organisation or brand, tables/infographics for comparisons and statistics.
Battles, summits, matches and other major events get the single most iconic image, not a montage.
Images are shown at native aspect ratio centred on black, with hard cuts and no motion.
Emotional beats may use an evocative period photograph; opinions, definitions and abstract reflection stay on black.

examples.transcript_window: Right in the middle of Gwanghwamun Square in Seoul sits a huge golden statue of a king. That's King Sejong the Great, the fourth king of the Joseon dynasty, and he ruled from Gyeongbokgung Palace just behind it. Honestly, most Koreans would tell you he's the greatest king in their history, and I think that's fair. In 1443 he created Hangul, the Korean alphabet, and published it in a document called the Hunminjeongeum.
